title: Leo Baeck in Theresienstadt
hookLine: Rabbi Leo Baeck kept teaching and lecturing as a prisoner in Theresienstadt
carry: the Shema says teach, even on the hardest road
tomorrow: who says Kaddish for a mother with no sons?

cards: While they packed the last shelf, Saba David, eyes wet, kept quizzing Noa on the Latin names of his old pharmacy jars. Why teach on a day like that?
This next story goes somewhere dark, so gently, with no details for small ears. Rabbi Leo Baeck was a leader of Germany's Jews in the Nazi years.

He's remembered for refusing chances to leave while his community still needed him. Then he was sent as a prisoner to Theresienstadt. And there, among exhausted people who could not leave, he kept teaching.
He gave lectures, on philosophy and on history. Why?

teach.b: Here's the wisdom-day question: what is teaching for, when it can't open the gate? Baeck's answer was the lectures themselves. A room listening to an idea is a room of people who still think, ask and argue.
The camp could take homes, names and bread.
A lecture said: your mind is still yours, and you are still a person, not a number. The Torah asks teaching of everyone, everywhere.

Deuteronomy says: "thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thy house, and when thou walkest by the way." Not only at school. On the way, wherever the way goes.
Now a neighbor who says something close. Noa's friend Owen, carrying boxes, remembered a line from his confirmation class.

teach.h: THE WORD OF GOD IS NOT BOUND.
teach.b: A New Testament letter, written in Paul's name from prison, says: "I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound." Shared: the teaching keeps going when the teacher is chained.

teach.h: THE SHEMA SAYS TEACH, EVEN ON THE HARDEST ROAD.
teach.b: The honest difference: for that letter, the word that isn't bound is the gospel of Christ. For Baeck, it was Torah, and with it the long human conversation of philosophy and history. Neither needs the other to be wrong.

how: Jewish communities remember Leo Baeck as a teacher and leader who stayed with his people; the duty to teach, from Deuteronomy 6:7, is recited daily in the Shema.

games.q: what does “teaching to the end” mean?
o: keeping on teaching others even in the worst conditions
finishing every lesson before you take on another
teaching one class from its first day to its last

games.q: your study partner's mom is in the hospital, and she wants to cancel your weekly Torah study: 'what's the point right now?' what would Baeck's lectures suggest?
o: offer a short, gentle session; learning can keep her whole on a hard week.
cancel; Torah study belongs to calm, easy times.
insist on the full session; skipping study is a failure.
games.why: Baeck kept teaching where no one could leave, and the Shema asks for teaching 'when thou walkest by the way'. learning isn't only for easy days.

practice: Choose one thing you know well: a recipe, a rule of a game, a line of Torah, a way to calm down. Say it out loud, slowly, in three or four sentences, as if teaching someone who's having a hard day and needs it.

wordCard.voice: Teaching to the end: Rabbi Leo Baeck lecturing to prisoners in Theresienstadt, because a mind still learning is a person still free inside.

orig.note: Hebrew: and you shall teach them diligently (Deuteronomy 6:7), words said daily in the Shema.

carryVoice: The line for today: the shema says teach, even on the hardest road. Leo Baeck did, where no one could leave.
